source.subject: Biology
source.unit: Unit 1 — Diversity in the Living World
source.source_scope: Only the content printed on PDF page 7 (printed page 16): the four groups of protozoans (amoeboid, flagellated, ciliated, sporozoans), the start of Section 2.3 Kingdom Fungi, hyphae and mycelium, and the nutrition and start of reproduction in fungi.

questions.question: Amoeboid protozoans move and capture their prey by putting out:
questions.explanation: The page says they put out pseudopodia, as in Amoeba.
questions.source_text: their prey by putting out pseudopodia (false feet) as in Amoeba.

questions.question: Marine forms of amoeboid protozoans have on their surface:
questions.explanation: The page says marine forms have silica shells on their surface.
questions.source_text: Marine forms have silica shells on their surface.

questions.question: Which of the following is a parasitic amoeboid protozoan named on the page?
questions.explanation: The page says some amoeboid protozoans such as Entamoeba are parasites.
questions.source_text: Some of them such as Entamoeba are parasites.

questions.question: Parasitic flagellated protozoans cause diseases such as:
questions.explanation: The page says parasitic flagellates cause diseases such as sleeping sickness, with Trypanosoma as the example.
questions.source_text: The parasitic forms cause diaseases such as sleeping sickness. Example: Trypanosoma.

questions.question: Ciliated protozoans are actively moving aquatic organisms because of:
options: The presence of thousands of cilia
questions.explanation: The page attributes their active movement to thousands of cilia.
questions.source_text: These are aquatic, actively moving organisms because of the presence of thousands of cilia.

questions.question: In ciliated protozoans, the coordinated movement of rows of cilia:
options: Steers water laden with food into the gullet
questions.explanation: The page says the coordinated movement of cilia steers the food-laden water into the gullet, a cavity opening to the outside of the cell surface.
questions.source_text: causes the water laden with food to be steered into the gullet.

questions.question: Sporozoans are diverse organisms that have:
options: An infectious spore-like stage in their life cycle
questions.explanation: The page says sporozoans have an infectious spore-like stage in their life cycle.
questions.source_text: This includes diverse organisms that have an infectious spore-like stage in their life cycle.

questions.question: The most notorious sporozoan, which causes malaria, is:
questions.explanation: The page names Plasmodium, the malarial parasite, as the most notorious sporozoan.
questions.source_text: The most notorious is Plasmodium (malarial parasite) which causes malaria

questions.question: Match each group of protozoans with its example from this page.
questions.explanation: Amoeba is amoeboid, Trypanosoma flagellated, Paramoecium ciliated and Plasmodium a sporozoan.
questions.source_text: as in Amoeba. ... Example: Trypanosoma. ... Example: Paramoecium (Figure 2.4d). ... The most notorious is Plasmodium

questions.question: Which unicellular fungus is used to make bread and beer?
questions.explanation: The page says some unicellular fungi, for example yeast, are used to make bread and beer.
questions.source_text: Some unicellular fungi, e.g., yeast are used to make bread and beer.

questions.question: Wheat rust is caused by which fungus, as given on the page?
questions.explanation: The page cites wheat rust-causing Puccinia as an important example of a fungus causing plant disease.
questions.source_text: wheat rust-causing Puccinia is an important example.

questions.question: Which fungus is mentioned on the page as a source of antibiotics?
questions.explanation: The page says some fungi are sources of antibiotics, for example Penicillium.
questions.source_text: Some are the source of antibiotics, e.g., Penicillium.

questions.question: Fungi prefer to grow in:
questions.explanation: The page says fungi prefer warm and humid places, which is why food is kept in a refrigerator.
questions.source_text: They prefer to grow in warm and humid places.

questions.question: With the exception of yeasts, fungi are:
questions.explanation: The page says that apart from unicellular yeasts, fungi are filamentous with bodies of thread-like hyphae.
questions.source_text: With the exception of yeasts which are unicellular, fungi are filamentous.

questions.question: The network of hyphae in a fungus is known as:
questions.explanation: The page says hyphae are long slender thread-like structures and their network is the mycelium.
questions.source_text: The network of hyphae is known as mycelium.

questions.question: Hyphae that are continuous tubes filled with multinucleated cytoplasm are called:
questions.explanation: The page defines coenocytic hyphae this way and says other hyphae have septae or cross walls.
questions.source_text: Some hyphae are continuous tubes filled with multinucleated cytoplasm – these are called coenocytic hyphae.

questions.question: The cell walls of fungi are composed of:
questions.explanation: The page states fungal cell walls are composed of chitin and polysaccharides.
questions.source_text: The cell walls of fungi are composed of chitin and polysaccharides.

questions.question: Match each term with its meaning as given on the page.
column_b: A. Fungi associated with roots of higher plants
B. Fungi absorbing soluble organic matter from dead substrates
C. Fungi depending on living plants and animals
questions.explanation: Saprophytes use dead substrates, parasites depend on living hosts, and symbionts form lichens with algae or mycorrhiza with roots of higher plants.
questions.source_text: absorb soluble organic matter from dead substrates and hence are called saprophytes. ... in association with algae as lichens and with roots of higher plants as mycorrhiza.

questions.question: Which are the means of vegetative reproduction in fungi mentioned on the page?
questions.explanation: The page lists fragmentation, fission and budding.
questions.source_text: Reproduction in fungi can take place by vegetative means – fragmentation, fission and budding.
